title: The hem of his garment (Mark 5:21–34)
hook: a woman bleeding twelve years touches his cloak in the crowd; he stops to find her

segments.voice: Yesterday, a healed man begged to follow and was sent home instead. Your line was go home and tell. Who heard your good news? Day one hundred seventy-eight.

Back across the lake, a crowd is waiting. A synagogue leader named Jairus pushes through, falls at Jesus's feet and begs: my little daughter is dying. Come. And Jesus goes, with the whole crowd pressing around him, shoulder to shoulder, jostling down a narrow street. Everyone's in a hurry. A child's life is on the line. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. She's been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything she had on doctors, and she's only gotten worse. She doesn't want a scene. She just wants to reach one hand through. Today: the hem of his garment.
screen: `JAIRUS: MY DAUGHTER IS DYING.` → `A CRUSH OF PEOPLE.` → `ONE HAND REACHES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Mark gives her story more detail than almost anyone's. In the old King James Bible she "had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse." Anyone who's fought with a long illness, or a medical bill, knows that sentence. Under the purity laws of the time, a condition like hers also made ordinary life complicated: worship, touch, closeness. So she makes a quiet plan. "If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole." She touches his cloak from behind, and immediately the bleeding stops. She can feel it. And here's the turn. Jesus stops. In the middle of an emergency, with a dying child waiting, he stops and asks, "Who touched my clothes?" His disciples almost laugh: look at this crowd, and you ask who touched you? But he keeps looking. And she comes forward, shaking, falls down, and tells him the whole truth. Then comes the first word he says to her: "Daughter." In Mark, she's the only person he calls that. "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." He could have let her slip away healed. Instead he made sure she was seen, named family, and sent off in peace in front of everyone. And notice the numbers. She's been ill twelve years. Jairus's daughter, we'll learn tomorrow, is twelve years old. Mark wraps one story inside the other on purpose. One more small thing: the hem in today's title comes from Matthew and Luke. Mark just says his clothes.
screen: `MANY PHYSICIANS, NOTHING BETTERED.` · `IF I MAY TOUCH BUT HIS CLOTHES.` · `WHO TOUCHED MY CLOTHES?` · `DAUGHTER, GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stop for someone the crowd ignores. Settle, and breathe. Picture a crowd you move through every day. A hallway, a store, a street, a group chat. Now look for the person nobody's looking at. The one who's been tired for years. The one who reaches out quietly and then pulls back. Let one face come. Imagine stopping. Turning around. Asking a real question and waiting for the whole truth. If you pray, you can pray for that person now. The bell holds the time.
The hem of his garment. What a woman ill for twelve years reached for in the crowd, and the reason he stopped to find her.
screen: `THE HEM OF HIS GARMENT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: daughter, go in peace. Today, stop for one person you'd usually hurry past, and make sure they feel seen. Day one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for the chronically ill with this story in mind, and some churches offer prayer for healing with the laying on of hands or anointing with oil, alongside medical care.

original.note: Greek: the outer cloak, the garment she touched in Mark.

trapdoor: what you thought: a woman is healed by touching a robe.
what it means: he stops a whole crowd, in an emergency, so that a woman nobody saw is seen, named daughter and sent in peace.
what a scholar hears: Mark wraps her story inside Jairus's, twelve years and a twelve-year-old, one of his favorite storytelling moves.

notes: Purity laws (Leviticus 15:25–27) phrased carefully ('made ordinary life complicated'); scholars caution against overstating her exclusion or framing Judaism negatively. Confirm tone.
'In Mark, she's the only person he calls daughter': confirm (Mark 5:34 is the only direct address as 'daughter' in Mark).
Mark 5:27 'touched his garment' (himation); 'hem/border' (kraspedon) is in Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44. Confirm.
The Markan 'sandwich' (5:21–43) and the twelve/twelve link; standard observation.
